keyFindings.description: The hand-back window is judged before the SUB is sent, not once the server has it. begin returns nil when FlushTimeout fails, so the term keeps the 3 s cap and its handle goroutine starts the hold while nats.go sends the SUB only after reconnecting, past the stopping pod's 1.25 s floor; resubscribe's SetReceiving then clears ack_wait_owed because handedBack is still true. A flush that succeeds after 250 ms-1 s is accepted the same way though the design leaves the SUB 250 ms. Judge the window when the flush returns; on a flush error or past the window, call HandBackLapsed and use the 7 s cap (t.hold is read only by handle).

When handBack's Release times out (2 s), the linger reads its own unreleased record as not taken, ends at the floor and drains; Stop's second Release (now reliable since item 2) then writes the record released and unsettled with ack_wait_owed as the term stands, after the subscription is gone. A standby taking it within 1 s counts a hand-back and holds 3 s with no linger behind it. Only the lapse check usually adds ack_wait_owed, by coincidence of the numbers; a renew that started at stop() and succeeded in just under 2 s extends validity past the late write. On a failed release, record the term's ack-wait debt before lingering.

The hand-back judgement is split across the lease boundary: leaseStatus.HandedBack, leaseStatus.handBack, lease.handedBack, lease.handBack and serve's local, with a two-call protocol (HandedBackAt then HandBackLapsed) and the receiver's time.Now() against the lease's injected l.now(). One lease method that judges and clears under l.mu with l.now().
